cells.tense: The stretch ahead isn't here yet and you're already standing in it, keeping your footing with what you've got.
cells.ask: Say out loud today what this load is for, to the one who benefits most from it — naming it turns private strength into something you can point to and they can meet you at.
cells.core:
On a plain afternoon here, you feel the weight of the thing and keep your footing anyway: the person you help gets steadier, the plan you carry holds when someone leans on it, and people around you relax because you don't flinch at the load. You're not managing how it looks — you're doing it, and you can feel that it's yours.

The strength is real and close to hand, but it hasn't been said out loud. Saying what it's for, in the open, is the one move left, and it keeps the work from being something you do alone in a room.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding the line, and you know you're the one holding it.
cells.place: the part of you that picks what you're going toward

cells.tense: Some future trouble hasn't arrived and you're already braced for it, holding harder than the thing in front of you needs.
cells.ask: Hand one thing back to the person who gave it, or tell the person you're carrying this for that you'd rather carry it together than alone — letting one load down to a fair weight lets the strength stay yours instead of eating you.
cells.core:
When this part is going well, work comes back in roughly what you put in. You give what you can and take help when it's offered, the exchange stays even, and nobody ends up keeping score — you give, they give, and both sides can stop counting.

The effort keeps outrunning what's actually being asked of you. You're holding more than the moment calls for, and the bracing is costing the very things it's meant to protect. The grip is doing the work, and nothing is coming back the other way.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding harder than the moment calls for, and it's costing you.

cells.tense: Something ended a while back and you're still standing at the closed door, holding what's already finished as if it were still going.
cells.ask: Tell one person today what this took from you — the hours, the worry, the thing you set down — and let their hearing it stand as part of the record, so the release arrives as rest instead of quitting.
cells.core:
At this part's best, you can carry a finished thing with both hands and still say, honestly, that it's finished — you set it down and feel the room, because the ending is complete and you're allowed to notice. You pick what you're going toward, and you know when the going is over.

The trouble is that you kept holding after the carry was done, so the strength has nothing left to hold against. You're still bracing at a door that's already shut. Saying what it took, to someone who can hear it, lets the last weight come off instead of being gripped tighter.
cells.sheetLine: The carrying is finished. You haven't put it down.
cells.place: the part of you that picks what you're going toward

cells.tense: You're holding more than you say you are, and you speak of it as though it settled on you from outside.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're carrying and finish the sentence — 'I chose to do this because' — to someone who'll hear it, even if it's one line in a note you don't send; calling it your choice takes the strength back from the outside and puts it back in your hands.
cells.core:
On a good day here, you can stand in what you've carried long enough to feel steady about it — the effort is out in the open between you and the person, and it's easier to keep at it because you know it's yours to keep or hand back. You say 'I picked this' and mean it, and that's what makes the load bearable.

What's happening instead is that the strength is doing the work while you give yourself no credit for it. What you're carrying is yours, but you describe it as something that arrived from outside, which leaves you working without owning the work. Finishing the sentence is the way back.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying this by choice and calling it something that happened to you.
cells.place: the part of you that picks what you're going toward

A reader might reasonably say 'this is just what working hard looks like' to the Too Much cell or 'I haven't had the space to hand anything over' to Too Little — the ask can hold either way, since naming a cost or showing one piece to one person doesn't need the guess to be true to be worth an hour. The sentences that came nearest to serving the writer over the reader were the pulls toward a vivid image; they were cut back to plain actions at a table.
